Molka Kammoun1 ● Paul Brady1 ● Luc De Catte2 ● Jan Deprest2 ● Koenraad Devriendt ● Joris Robert Vermeesch1 Received: 20 March 2017 / Revised: 26 September 2017 / Accepted: 17 October 2017 / Published online: 22 January 2018 © European Society of Human Genetics 2018 Abstract Nance–Horan syndrome is a rare Xlinked developmental disorder characterized by bilateral congenital cataract, dental anomalies, facial dysmorphism, and intellectual disability.
Here, we identify a patient with Nance–Horan syndrome caused by a new nonsense NHS variant.
In addition, the patient presented congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
NHS gene expression in murine fetal diaphragm was demonstrated, suggesting a possible involvement of NHS in diaphragm development.
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia could result from NHS loss of function in pleuroperitoneal fold or in somitesderived muscle progenitor cells leading to an impairment of their cells migration.
Introduction Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a lifethreatening condition affecting 2.3 per 10,000 births.

The malformation results from a defect of the muscular or of the tendinous portion of the diaphragm leading the abdominal viscera to herniate into the thoracic cavity and to compete for space with the developing lungs.
Clinically, CDH occurs either as an isolated malformation in approximately half of the cases, or in association with other malformations.
Cardiovascular defects are by far the most common associated malformations.
Less frequently, CDH is associated with musculoskeletal, urogenital, or brain malformations, and is rarely associated with ocular defects that effect about 1% of cases.
As summarized in Table 1, CDHassociated congenital eye malformations consist mainly of anophthalmia and microphthalmia in conjunction with colobomas.
Congenital cataract and late onset cataract have been described with CDH in one case of HCCS deletion and in a few cases of LRP2 mutation, respectively.
The genetics of CDH is still poorly understood.

In addition, CDH genetics is highly heterogeneous with at least 70 known CDH causal genes, making whole exome sequencing an attractive approach for CDH genetic causes identiﬁcation.
This approach is especially interesting for complex CDH cases, where it can help to identify potential novel CDH causal genes with pleotropic effects.
In this paper, whole exome sequencing was performed on a male fetus diagnosed with CDH and bilateral congenital cataracts and his two unaffected parents.
A likely pathogenic variant was identiﬁed in NHS.
